cards.title: Cold Email Structure: Opener and Value in One Message
cards.summary: Email outreach is more compact than DM, so the opener and the value offer should ship in the same email, kept personal, important-looking outside and personable inside.
cards.use_when: Writing the first cold outreach email to a store owner, brand founder or marketing lead you want to work with or partner with.
steps: Recognize that email, unlike Instagram DMs, is a compact channel — you do not get a separate 'opener' message and a later 'value' message with this prospect. Send both at once.
Make the outside look important and worth opening: curiosity-based subject line that includes their first name so it reads as personal rather than spam.
Write the inside as personal, witty and personable — not a dry, robotic pitch.
End the email with a single strong value offer that is easy to say yes to (a short video, a free asset, a small low-risk project), so the reply step requires almost no effort.
Warm the domain gradually over a long period rather than blasting volume immediately, so future emails don't land in the spam folder.
caveats: The source frames this for service outreach; the structure transfers to supplier, affiliate and wholesale-partner emails, but the value offer must be something the other party actually wants.

cards.title: Different Is Better Than Better in Cold Outreach
cards.summary: Everyone in a prospect's inbox is sending the same dry 'we'll get you X in 60 days' pitch, so the winning move is being different and witty rather than marginally better.
cards.use_when: Designing the angle and creative format for a cold outreach email to a brand or retailer, when your pitch otherwise looks identical to every competitor's.
steps: Look at what the standard pitch in your space looks like — typically a dry claim about views, revenue or results with a conditional guarantee — and treat that as the boring baseline you must not match.
Build the angle around your specific DNA, experiences and stories rather than around generic claims, since you are the one-of-one element no competitor can copy.
Use creative devices that break the pattern: a small personalized graphic, a witty line, a funny image, or a Loom video email as the value vehicle.
Keep all the underlying principles intact (personalization, justification for claims, easy reply CTA) — different is only better when the substance holds up.
caveats: This is the presenter's strong opinion on cold outreach; he explicitly says it only works alongside the rest of the principles taught. The same creative move sent to a different niche or personality type may miss — some recipients respond to witty, others find it dumb.

cards.title: Borrowed Authority Email: Make an Established Brand the Proof
cards.summary: Instead of asking a prospect to trust your judgment, point at a top player in their niche already doing the thing you recommend and position yourself as the path to matching them.
cards.use_when: Writing a mid-sequence outreach email or PDP/email critique to a store owner who has no reason yet to trust your recommendations.
steps: Identify a brand or operator in the prospect's own vertical that is visibly ahead of them and that they already recognize as an authority.
State the gap concretely: what the prospect's page, emails or funnel currently do versus what the top player's version does.
Frame the recommendation as a route to copying a known winner rather than as your personal opinion: 'the same systems used by [top player]'.
Give a short, low-friction CTA — offering a recorded walkthrough or sample asset they can review.
Keep the email shorter and straighter than a witty anti-pitch email; borrowed authority is a proof angle, so it does not need jokes.
caveats: Use a relevant, genuinely comparable authority figure — if the example is not someone the prospect respects or recognizes, the borrowed trust never lands.

cards.title: Straight-to-the-Point Outreach Email With Permission to Say No
cards.summary: A three-to-six line email that respects the prospect's time, adds risk reversal and explicitly gives permission to decline, which lowers pressure and often raises replies.
cards.use_when: Prospect is busy or senior, or you have tried longer/wittier outreach and want a no-frills variant for your email sequence.
steps: Open with an explicit time-respect line such as 'I value your time so I'll get straight to the point'.
State what you made and the time cost to the recipient: a Loom video, a short walkthrough, roughly three minutes.
Say what it will do for them in outcome terms (more conversions from the same traffic, more revenue with zero extra work).
Add risk reversal so saying yes costs them nothing.
Close with an easy micro-commitment and a pressure-release: reply 'yes' and you'll send it, and 'if not that's cool too, just let me know'.
Skip wit and jokes in this variant — it is the straight version, meant for buyers who respond to brevity.
caveats: Not a universal winner — the source presents this as one angle among several because different business owners respond to different tones.

cards.title: Breakup Email: Create Scarcity With the Last Message
cards.summary: A follow-up framed as the final email that tells the prospect you are about to delete the asset you made for them; the source reports this format generates a very high volume of replies.
cards.use_when: A prospect has gone cold after several outreach emails and you are choosing which final follow-up to send before stopping.
steps: Acknowledge directly that they've gone cold and that this is the last email on the subject.
State a concrete, near-term consequence to the asset: you'll be taking down the Loom video shortly after sending this.
Remind them what the asset covers — for example improvements to their headline or funnel that should lift conversions.
Give one frictionless reply instruction: reply 'yes' and it's sent over.
Keep the tone gracious rather than needy: if not, wish them luck with everything.
caveats: The source calls this the strongest reply-getting follow-up but the claim is anecdotal; the threat must stay plausible — deleting an asset you genuinely would remove — or it reads as a bluff.

cards.title: Follow-Up Is the Neglected Half of Outreach
cards.summary: The source argues follow-up matters as much as or more than the initial outreach and that inconsistent, un-followed-up outreach is the real reason people conclude outreach doesn't work.
cards.use_when: Scheduling your outreach cadence and deciding how many touches a prospect should receive before you stop, or when someone has replied but hasn't converted.
steps: Treat follow-up as a designed part of the sequence, not an optional add-on: plan multiple touches over time.
Come back from different angles each time (a new proof point, a different creative format, a different offer framing) rather than repeating the same message.
If a prospect replied at any point, do not let them go — a reply proves they are open to the offer once the timing is right.
Push discipline over cleverness: the failure mode is people completing steps only partially and then blaming outreach.
Accept that first attempts feel clunky and may not land a client immediately; the fix is completing the sequence and improving, not switching methods.
caveats: The presenter states this forcefully from his own experience as an agency owner; no numeric reply rates are established, so treat the intensity as his opinion, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Video Intro DM: Send Video or Voice Note Instead of Text
cards.summary: Stand out from text-only DMs by sending a short video (or voice note) that introduces you on camera, states how you help, and offers either a call or free value.
cards.use_when: Instagram or social DM outreach to a brand or store owner, especially when most competitors are sending plain-text pitches.
steps: Open with a normal opener as you would for a text DM — warm and specific.
Instead of writing out your value pitch, record a short video or voice note introducing who you are, what you do, and how you can help them.

At the end of the video pitch either the call ('if that's something you'd be open to, let me know and we can hop on a call') or the value ('I made a longer walkthrough / sample email sequence — say the word and it's in your inbox in minutes').
In the thumbnail or first frame, put their name on the video so they can see it was made for them specifically.
Look presentable and speak articulately — the source says the on-camera competence is itself the social proof and authority signal.
Keep the script extremely simple; the presenter states his own script feels too simple to work and it still gets results.
caveats: Voice notes work but are explicitly stated to be less effective than video. The presenter warns this exact script has been widely shared, so copying it verbatim removes the differentiation — change it and make it your own.

cards.title: Loom Funnel Audit as an Outreach Value Offer
cards.summary: Walk a prospect's own marketing funnel, record a sub-four-minute Loom of concrete improvements plus proof for each claim, and offer it as the outreach asset.
cards.use_when: Cold outreach to an ecommerce brand where you can review their sales page, product page, email sequence or funnel for real improvement opportunities.
steps: Go through the prospect's funnel exactly as a customer would — landing/opt-in page, sales page copy, email sequence and email copy — and note where leads could be slipped.
Record a Loom video under four minutes; the presenter suggests roughly three as a practical max.
Give an alternative, not just a critique: pair each problem with a concrete better version to demonstrate you are providing value.
Justify every claim inside the video — say why a change will help and show the evidence, rather than asserting 'this would be better'.
Use a compliment sandwich: lead with what they did well and show you recognize them as the expert, give one or two critiques, then close on their strong points.
Reference your own past client results so the recommendations carry weight beyond your own assertion.
Turn on webcam bubble so they see a face tied to the audit.
caveats: The 'right' length is the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark; when recording, you can edit rather than nailing it in one take.

cards.title: Free Value Assets to Attach to Outreach: Email Sequence, Sales Page Sample, Funnel Audit
cards.summary: Three concrete value offers you can hand a prospect up front — a written email sequence, a sample sales page document, or a Loom funnel audit — each of which doubles as a proof of your ability.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to attach to a cold outreach for a store or brand, and trying to overcome the 'I don't know if you can sound like us' objection.
steps: Free email sequence: write a three-email sequence for them that matches their voice. This directly answers the biggest objection — whether you can sound like them — and if the emails are good they may simply use them, making you the writer going forward.
Free sales page example: produce a document showing what their sales page copy would look like if you wrote it, so they evaluate actual copy rather than a description of your service.
Loom funnel audit: record a walkthrough of their funnel with alternatives and proof behind each claim.
Combine assets when useful — the presenter sometimes writes a free sales page and records a Loom contrasting their current page with the rewrite.

Before choosing the asset, listen to what the prospect asks for; in the case study the prospect himself listed sequences he needed (event ticket sales, upsell, welcome/nurture, revival), which made the follow-up easy to scope.
caveats: These are the presenter's own closing examples from his practice; they show what worked for him, not guaranteed results. The work is free up front — you only convert if the quality holds.

cards.title: Answering Budget and Trust Objections With a Low-Risk First Project
cards.summary: Agree with the objection first, then shrink the scope to a small paid test project so the store can judge your work without a large commitment.
cards.use_when: A prospect says your quoted price is over budget or that they won't commit big without first seeing your quality — common on retainer or full-funnel quotes.
steps: Agree with the objection immediately ('totally understandable — that's a big commitment without seeing what I can do'); never argue that the deal is already good value, since that creates friction.
Reframe yourself as the one qualifying the fit as well: 'see if we're a good fit to work together' rather than 'let me show you how good I am'.

Propose a single small low-risk project with a concrete deliverable and price — in the case study, one eight-email sequence for $400 when the prospect balked at a ~50–60 email project. Treat this as a big-fish-on-the-rod move you can expand from, not a market rate.
Once working, keep scope discussion going through their actual needs list so you can price by volume with a discount structure if it makes sense.
Set clear per-unit pricing when the volume is large (in the case study, $150/email standard with a reduction to $100/email at volume) so the comparison is legible.
caveats: All dollar figures are this presenter's own case study and not benchmarks. He states he can't script every negotiation because each conversation differs — use the pattern (agree, de-risk, reduce scope), not the exact numbers.

cards.title: Circle Back After a Decline: The 'We Already Have Someone' Reply Is a Win
cards.summary: A decline, including 'we already have someone', is worth reusing: people move roles, and the replacement needs a provider — so follow up months later around their new launch.
cards.use_when: A store or brand has turned down your outreach or says they already have a writer/agency for content, SEO, product copy or email.
steps: Read 'we already have somebody for that' as a good signal — they engaged, which means they are open to your type of offer.
Do not push back on the decline; let them know to reach out if that changes.
Track them and re-approach roughly one, two, three months later — most people change positions or move companies within a year, and the replacement usually needs a provider.
Anchor the re-approach to something current and observable: a new product launch, promotion, challenge or marketing channel they just started ('I saw you recently launched X').
Make a light, low-commitment CTA around that new activity: offer free value against their new product or a short call about the new channel.
Stay top of mind so that when the need appears you are the obvious choice to contact.
caveats: The presenter describes this from his experience as a business owner and says most people misread the decline as a loss; the timeline is his observed pattern, not a guaranteed outcome.

cards.title: Anti-Spam Outreach: Personalize Every Message
cards.summary: A DM that announces it is bot-blasted, gets the niche wrong and uses no personalization actively repels the prospect and gets remembered as spam.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own outreach before sending, or when designing a scalable outreach process and tempted to automate the messaging.
steps: Check the recipient: the example bad DM pitched email marketing to a non-fitness prospect while claiming a fitness niche — mismatched targeting wastes everyone's time.

Do not tell the prospect you are spamming: the bad example literally said 'I'm sending thousands of cold DMs and don't have time for warm DMs' — the source argues that self-disqualifies you from fulfilling the work.
Cut volume-first language like 'I have 70 prepared emails, hopefully you need email marketing' — it communicates you haven't looked at them.
Personalize with something only a real reader would know: reply to their recent story content, reference a specific post, or ask a specific question about their funnel.
Before sending, ask whether the recipient would read this and think 'this is exactly what I need' — if not, rewrite the angle.
caveats: The source presents this as what-not-to-do from an actual DM he received; the lesson is about personalization, not about banning automation tooling itself.

cards.title: Set Up Your Social Profile So the Prospect Pitches You
cards.summary: A profile showing what you do and who you've helped can turn a bare opener into the prospect asking to buy before you ever pitch.
cards.use_when: Preparing your social profile before starting DM outreach so that your opener does the minimum and the profile does the selling.
steps: Define your bio around three things: what you do, how you do it, and who you've helped before.
Keep the opener minimal — the case study opener was just a general compliment ('love the real estate and wealth gems'), which the presenter admits wasn't specific.
Let the profile carry the pitch: in that case the prospect replied asking about email copy pricing without the sender ever mentioning copywriting.
Note the counterpoint: the presenter says if he repeated the outreach he would write a better, more specific opener — the profile covers the gap, but a specific opener is still stronger.
Apply the same principle to your storefront equivalents — profile, pinned content, and public portfolio links — since they are legible the moment someone checks who messaged them.
caveats: The source's example is personal-brand DM outreach, not ecommerce; the transferable part is making your public profile a proof asset, not the exact bio.

cards.title: Stop Asking Outreach Advice and Pick One Method to Master
cards.summary: The source argues there is no secret outreach method; the winning method is the one you actually stick with, and advice-seeking questions are usually a substitute for doing the work.
cards.use_when: You are choosing which outreach channel to commit to for a store's wholesale, partnership or service outreach and feel tempted to keep researching alternatives.
steps: Pick one of the known methods — cold email, video intro DM, Loom funnel audit — and run it consistently rather than swapping methods after a few attempts.
Expect the first attempts to feel clunky and not to land immediately; that is part of learning the skill, not evidence the method is broken.
When tempted to look for an advanced or secret method, redirect the time into improving the value you send.
Remember the presenter's framing that most competitors never finish the steps at all — the field of people who actually execute is far smaller than the field who talk about it.
Build the copywriting skill and the outreach skill at the same time, since each improves the other's output.
Give it weeks or months of consistent execution; the presenter frames the timeline loosely and explicitly says there is luck in the short term that long-term volume mitigates.
caveats: This is the presenter's strongly stated opinion, including his claim that no secret method exists. Treat the timeline ('a couple weeks, maybe a couple months') as his experience, not a promise.

cards.title: Steal the Ideas, Not the Words, from Outreach Templates
cards.summary: Copy-pasting outreach templates word for word gets recognised instantly; change the phrasing drastically so your message doesn't look like something the prospect has already seen.
cards.use_when: Using any outreach template or swipe file for ecommerce partner or brand outreach before sending it.
steps: Make a personal copy of every template file you use — in Google Drive, use File > Make a copy rather than requesting access — so your edits stay yours.
Treat the template's structure (opener, proof, value offer, CTA, permission to decline) as the reusable part.
Rewrite the words: change the phrasing, the specific reference, the joke and the deliverable, so it reads as written for this recipient.
Recognise that templates widely shared on the internet circulate to the same prospects; a verbatim send signals you're a beginner and makes the prospect unwilling to work with you.

Keep the specificity check: a line that works for a sales coach (I've been watching your sales advice, it helped me close a deal) is wrong for a fitness or dating coach — the idea travels, the words don't.
caveats: The presenter shares many templates himself and acknowledges that even with volume, duplication is likely; the fix is deliberate rewriting, not template avoidance.

cards.title: Retell the Story, Don't Relive It (Story Email Structure for Ecommerce)
cards.summary: For story-driven emails, open with the result, relate the problem, bridge the gap and close on the dream state — and write scenes the reader can relive rather than a summary retold.
cards.use_when: Writing a customer story, founder story or testimonial email for a store's list, or crediting a brand's email sequences in a funnel audit.
steps: Start with the 'what's in it for me': lead with the big result up front, not buried in the subject line alone — e.g. 'six months later she was doing $125k launching and working fewer hours — here's how'.
Then go back to the problem and agitate it, moving the story through: problem, who the student/person is, where they are now, the bridge (how they got there), then the dream state at the end.
Give the reader a CTA at the end pointing to more information.

Write to relive rather than retell: instead of 'I was working long hours for low pay with no promotion, so I started a business', write the scene — 'one day I worked hard labour until my back throbbed; I was 20 but felt 59; the boss said work harder; that's when I started my business today'.
Use a structured checklist for your own story emails so the critique and the writing stay organised, and note precise line-level changes rather than general praise.
caveats: The included $125k example is a client's case study, not a promise. The structure is the transferable part; do not fabricate testimonial results to fit the shape.

cards.title: Loom Video Audit Delivery: Compliment Sandwich and Justification
cards.summary: In a funnel-audit video, compliment first, critique with proof, and justify every change by referencing past client results or a borrowed authority rather than asserting your judgment.
cards.use_when: Recording a value Loom for a store's sales page, email sequence or automation flow, or walking them through a proposed test.
steps: Lead with what they did well and show you recognise them as the expert — this keeps the critique from reading as an attack.
Give one or two concrete critiques, each paired with an alternative version and a justification for why it would help.
Reference your own past results or the results of a known authority running the same strategy, so the claim rests on something other than your assertion.
Show the evidence on screen where possible — e.g. the prospect's own emails sitting in the promotions tab — before explaining the deliverability implication and the fix.
Close on their strengths again so the video stays constructive.
Keep the recording structured; the presenter uses a written resource during the Loom so the delivery is organised rather than hesitant, and edits the take afterwards.
caveats: Length and structure are presenter heuristics; he sometimes runs longer on purpose to give more to choose from, but states around three minutes as the target.

cards.title: Talking About Your Work: Use a Unique Frame, Not a Crowded Label
cards.summary: The presenter avoids calling himself a copywriter because the label is crowded with unskilled beginners; he uses a differentiating frame like 'digital marketer specialising in done-for-you marketing systems' instead.
cards.use_when: Writing your outreach bio, profile description or pitch line for a store or brand, and choosing how to describe what you do.
steps: Identify the label you'd default to and ask whether it is diluted in your niche — the source's example is 'copywriter', which he says many unskilled beginners claim.
Replace it with a frame that describes the outcome and mechanism: specialising in done-for-you email and marketing systems, or direct-response copywriting, rather than the generic role name.
Carry that frame consistently through your profile, videos and emails so the prospect's first impression is about capability, not category.
Use the frame as a differentiator, the same way a product uses a unique mechanism to stand out from an identical commodity.
caveats: This is the presenter's own positioning choice from his practice, not a rule; it works because he can back the frame with demos and past results.

cards.title: Rate and Scope Email Work by Sequencing a Client's Real Needs
cards.summary: When a prospect lists the sequences they need, translate that list into a volume-and-price quote, treat a large project as a big-fish opportunity, and use fixed per-email pricing as the anchor.
cards.use_when: Quoting a store or brand that asks for multiple email flows — welcome/nurture, cart recovery, event or launch promotions, revival campaigns — as one engagement.
steps: Get the prospect to enumerate needs concretely: in the case study the client listed event ticket sales emails, an after-event upsell sequence, a welcome sequence for one audience, a nurture campaign for another, and a revival campaign for the existing database.
Count the total units (the example totalled 50+ emails) so you can price by volume instead of guessing per project.
Quote a per-unit rate and then, for genuinely large volumes, offer a volume discount — the case study went from $150/email to $100/email, presenting the reduction as fair given the size.
If the total is rejected, split off a smaller sequence as the paid test (see the low-risk first-project approach).
When confirming scope in writing, restate exactly what is included so there is no ambiguity when the emails are delivered.
caveats: All figures are the presenter's own case-study pricing and not market benchmarks; the operative move is transparent volume-based pricing, not the specific rate.

cards.title: Warm Up Cold Outreach With Story Replies Before the Pitch
cards.summary: Reply to a prospect's story with a genuine, specific reaction, then let a few days pass before sending the video intro and pitch — this softens the message and can get you invited to pitch.
cards.use_when: Planning a multi-touch outreach sequence on Instagram to a brand founder whose content you already follow.
steps: Reply to a recent piece of their content with something specific and sincere about it — the case study replies were short lines like 'this is really smart marketing' or 'I never thought about it that way before'.
Let the reply sit for a couple of days rather than pitching straight away.
Follow with the video intro DM that introduces you, what you do, and how you can help.

If they respond with openness, ask one diagnostic question about their setup — the case study asked whether anyone on their team currently handles the marketing side — then follow up with a low-pressure call ask if no answer.
If they redirect you elsewhere (another person, email, an application form for a different role), keep the thread alive and re-anchor to the role you actually want.
caveats: The case study includes a $3k/month result and clients found this way, but that is one example, not a benchmark. Some prospects delegate DMs to salespeople, so be ready to be routed.

cards.title: Warm List-to-Email Handoff: Be Ready With Sample Work and Portfolio
cards.summary: When a DM contact routes you to a manager or inbox, be prepared to hand over email samples and a portfolio immediately — that handoff is often what converts.
cards.use_when: You are doing social outreach to a brand and they ask you to email someone internally, or they request work samples.
steps: Expect the handoff: a DM reply like 'too busy, email this person' is a path forward, not a rejection.
Have email samples ready to send the moment they ask, so the conversation doesn't stall on your production time.
Maintain a portfolio link and be ready to say what other copy you write — in the case study the request was specifically for portfolio plus non-email copy types.
Offer to discuss small projects as the next step, framing it as seeing whether you're a good fit rather than pushing for the biggest scope.
Expect practical steps like NDAs and briefs, and keep moving — the same case study closed a 10-email sequence at $2,000 with around 30–40 minutes of work per email.
caveats: The $2,000 / 10-email figure is a specific case study, not a rate card. The presenter also notes the buyer asked him to quote per email only after the deal was agreed — arrange pricing clarity earlier if you can.
